To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

wood-eating loricariid fishes have robust jaws specialized for chewing wood, elevated d 15N values and consume cellulose from wood, whereas two surface-feeding loricariid fish species have different jaw morphologies and consume different food sources.

the jaw morphology of Neotropical catfishes is correlated with their feeding behavior and that the carbon and nitrogen isotopic signatures of catfishes and their prey indicate that these catfishes are specialized to feed in different habitats and on different prey.

the seven species of loricariids examined in this study occupy divergent regions of morphological space and that they have divergent isotopic signatures, consistent with the hypothesis that they partition their niche by feeding on different food resources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of fishes in the ecology and conservation of streams.
the ecology of the fishes that inhabit the rivers of the world, particularly those of the tropics.
the role of fishes in the decomposition of coarse particulate organic material (CPOM), particularly wood, in streams.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the wood-grazing fishes partition their niches.
wood‐grazing Neotropical fishes are partitioned in their niche by trophic segregation, and that this segregation is based on jaw morphological and isotopically determined food resources.
wood‐grazing loricariids partition their niche.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
wood‐grazing fish in Neotropical streams partition their niche by using different jaw morphologies for feeding.
the wood-grazing fishes partition their niches, and the partitioning is based on their jaw morphologies and their trophic niches.
the wood-eating catfishes in this study have a unique set of functional traits that allow them to feed on wood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
wood-eating catfishes are not all created equal.

wood-eating loricariids have evolved a suite of convergent morphological and isotopically distinct trophic traits that are consistent with a diet of holocelluloses and other morphic detrital components of coarse woody detritus, and that wood-eating species partition their trophic niche with non-wood-eater species in a tropical river.
wood-eating fishes in Neotropical river systems are not a single, monophyletic group.
